name: Bilal Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bilal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead carpenter at Hartley and Sons, a family firm, about fourteen of us, and we do renovations on old houses. Victorian terraces mostly, some older. Right now I'm rebuilding a staircase in a house on Elm Row where the last owner tried to fix it with screws and hope. My day is a lot of standing and looking before I cut anything, because in an old house nothing is square, nothing is level, and every wall has a secret.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last month I took the plaster off a wall and found a whole doorway somebody bricked up a hundred years ago, with the old frame still in it. You learn to read a house, where it's moved, where the water's been. That's the part I'm good at. The part I hate is the paperwork Hartley's son keeps bringing in, forms on a tablet, photos for this, photos for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, right, can we get back to work now. I've never used any of it and I don't plan to. I'd say it at the tea break and that would be the end of the conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing to me either way. Nobody was ever going to send a computer to fix a staircase on Elm Row. Maybe it means young Hartley stops bringing in new apps every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing now. Finish the staircase, start the sash windows on the next job, pay the mortgage, take the kids to the coast in August. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad the noise would stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has any of the new tech at Hartley's actually helped you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The laser level, I'll give them that, but that's not AI, that's just a good tool. The app for photos, no. It takes me twenty minutes at the end of the day, and Niamh says I come home grumpier on Fridays because of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be most disappointed, if AI was all hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young Hartley, Tom. He's thirty and he thinks every problem has an app. He'd sulk for a week. His dad, old Frank, would laugh, because Frank still writes quotes on the back of an envelope.

S0.say: Right, can we get back to work now? I've never used any of it and don't plan to, and I'd say that at the tea break and leave it there.
S0.think: It means nothing to me either way, because nobody was sending a computer to fix a staircase on Elm Row. Maybe it means the boss's son stops bringing in a new app every month.
S0.do: Finishes the Elm Row staircase and moves on to sash windows at the next job. Keeps paying the mortgage and takes the family to the coast in August as planned.
S0.feel: Calm and glad the noise would stop.
S0.quote: Nobody was ever going to send a computer to fix a staircase on Elm Row.
S0.fieldNote: Bilal sees AI as noise from the office side, mostly the boss's son and his apps. He's practical rather than ideological about it. His pride is in reading old houses, which he doesn't think a machine could ever do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll change the new-build sites, not us. Old houses are too awkward. I'd say that to the lads and I think most of them would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd keep an eye on it. If the firm starts using machines to measure and quote, fine, but I don't want to be told how to cut a stair by a screen. I think I'd be all right, though, I'm the one they call when something's gone wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd keep my head down and see what Hartley's brings in. If they made me use some new gadget I'd learn the bare minimum, the same as I did with the photo app. I wouldn't go looking for courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little grumpy about more forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the bare minimum. What if the bare minimum isn't enough one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn a bit more, I'm not stupid. But I'm not going to chase it. I've seen enough fashions on building sites to know half of them disappear in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What fashion did you see disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plastic plumbing push-fit systems, about fifteen years back, everyone said copper was finished. Half of them leaked. Now we're back to copper in the old houses. I'm not saying AI is a fad, but I like to wait and see.

S1.say: It'll change the new-build sites, not us, because old houses are too awkward. I'd say that to the lads and most of them would agree.
S1.think: I'd keep an eye on it, and I don't want a screen telling me how to cut a stair. I think I'd be fine because I'm the one they call when something's gone wrong.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and waits to see what the firm brings in. Learns only the bare minimum of any required new tool and doesn't seek out courses.
S1.feel: Calm, a little grumpy about more forms.
S1.quote: I've seen enough fashions on building sites to know half of them disappear in five years.
S1.fieldNote: His confidence rests on the awkwardness of old houses and his role as the fixer. He uses past fads, like a plumbing system that leaked, to justify waiting. He's not hostile, just unwilling to chase change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see a robot get up a Victorian staircase. That's what I'd say out loud, anyway. I'd probably make a joke about it at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it would frighten me. Two years is nothing. If a machine can really do anything a person can, then sooner or later it can read a wall too, and I'm forty-three with a mortgage, two kids and about two months of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away: no coast trip, no new van, cancel the sports channels. I'd ask Frank Hartley straight out what he's planning and whether I've got a job in a year. I'd probably try to take on extra weekend jobs while people still want a human, to build some savings. And if it came to it, I'd ask my brother for help, he's got a bit put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone soft under me. I don't panic, but I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Niamh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we'd manage, which is what I always say. She works in the pharmacy on the high street, and I'd be wondering if a machine counts pills too. That's the bit that would keep me up, both of us going at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd joke about it in the pub but be frightened at home. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what you do. Nobody wants to hear a grown man say he's scared at the bar. I'd say it to Niamh in the kitchen, nobody else.

S2.say: I don't believe it until I see a robot get up a Victorian staircase. I'd say that out loud and probably make a joke of it at the pub.
S2.think: It would frighten me, because two years is nothing and if a machine can do anything, sooner or later it can read a wall too. I'm forty-three with a mortgage, two kids and about two months saved.
S2.do: Cancels the coast trip, the new van and the sports channels straight away. Asks his boss directly about his job, takes extra weekend work to build savings and would ask his brother for help if needed.
S2.feel: Frightened and losing sleep, though he wouldn't show it in public.
S2.quote: Nobody wants to hear a grown man say he's scared at the bar.
S2.fieldNote: Bilal's public line is disbelief, but privately the two-year picture shakes him badly. The real fear is both household incomes going at once, since his wife works in a pharmacy. He would turn to family, his brother, before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years, let's see. I'd say it at work like it's weather, something that's coming, nothing you can do. I wouldn't post anything, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is better, but I'm still not going to be a different man at forty-eight. I'm a carpenter. If the work goes, the work goes, but I'd want to have the money right by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a bit more aside each month, a hundred or so, and stop spending on the house. I'd keep working at Hartley's as long as they'll have me. I'd not train for anything new, not yet, I'd want to see the robots actually working first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could live with it day to day. It'd sit at the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to see the robots working. How would you know when it's time to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When Frank takes one on. He's the slowest man in the trade, so if Frank buys a robot, it's real. That's my alarm clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got kids of eleven and seven. Would this change anything for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Aidan wants to come and work with me, he's always in the van on Saturdays. I'd still let him help, but I'd not promise him the trade. I'd say get your exams first, then we'll see.

S3.say: Five years, let's see. I'd talk about it at work like the weather, something coming that you can't do much about, and I wouldn't post anything.
S3.think: Five years is better, but I'm not going to be a different man at forty-eight. If the work goes, it goes, but I'd want the money right by then.
S3.do: Saves about 100 more each month and stops spending on the house. Stays at Hartley's and holds off on retraining until he sees robots actually working.
S3.feel: Anxious, but able to live with it day to day.
S3.quote: He's the slowest man in the trade, so if Frank buys a robot, it's real.
S3.fieldNote: He treats the change like weather and waits for a clear signal: his cautious boss buying a robot. He uses the time to save, not to retrain. His son's wish to join the trade makes him quietly hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and a lot can happen. Who knows. I'd say that and change the subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fifty-three. The mortgage would be close to done, Aidan would be grown, Sara would be seventeen. I think I'd be all right, if I'm careful, but I don't fancy starting over at fifty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on working and keep chipping away at the mortgage. Maybe in five or six years, if it looked real, I'd think about something like building inspection, where you still go and look at houses. Until then I'd keep doing what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a job you know is coming that you're putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Building inspection. Would you really do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. You're still reading houses, still going up in lofts. I wouldn't love the forms, but I'd love it more than stacking shelves. I'd only do it if I had to, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd want to do while there's still time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish my own house. I've been doing the stairs at home for six years, I'm the cobbler with no shoes. I'd like to get that done with my own hands before the robots turn up.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and a lot can happen, so who knows. I'd say that and then change the subject.
S4.think: I'd be fifty-three with the mortgage nearly done and the kids mostly grown, so I'd probably be fine if I'm careful. But I don't fancy starting over at fifty-three.
S4.do: Carries on working and keeps paying down the mortgage. Considers moving into building inspection in five or six years, but only if the change looks real.
S4.feel: Uneasy, like a job he keeps putting off.
S4.quote: I'd like to get that done with my own hands before the robots turn up.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his fear drops to a background worry because the mortgage and children are nearly through. He picks a fallback that keeps him close to old houses. Finishing his own staircase is a small, personal goal that says a lot about him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easy. In that one I'm out of work before I've even decided if I believe it. What would help is time, really, and some kind of wage while I learned something else, so we don't lose the house. I'm not asking for a handout, just a bridge to the next thing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that people like me don't talk about this stuff. I've never said any of this out loud before, not even to Niamh, not all of it. There's a lot of men on sites who are worried and just make jokes.

headlineQuote: There's a lot of men on sites who are worried and just make jokes.
portrait: Bilal Quinn is a 43-year-old lead carpenter at a small family firm that renovates Victorian houses, married to a pharmacy worker, with two children and about two months saved. He reads old houses for a living and has no interest in AI, putting up with the boss's son's apps only as far as he has to. He's calm under a plateau or steady change, confident old houses are too awkward for machines. The two-year AGI picture frightens him in private while he jokes in public, and with five or ten years he'd save and wait for a clear sign, perhaps moving into building inspection late on.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be out of work before he'd even decided whether he believed it.
whatWouldHelp: Time, and a wage while he learned something else, so the family doesn't lose the house: a bridge, not a handout.
